parsed.summary: The Lean theorem states that for any group α and any subgroup s, Nat.card s divides Nat.card α. There is no finiteness assumption, so it is formally stronger than the paper's statement. For finite α it is exactly Lagrange's theorem. For infinite α, Nat.card α = 0 and every natural number divides 0, so the extra cases hold only via the junk value. This is harmless.

glossary.plain: cardinality of a type as a natural number (|H|, |G|), with value 0 for infinite types
glossary.note: It agrees with the order on finite groups and is 0 on infinite ones. The paper only concerns finite G, so this does not matter.

lean_claims.plain: For every group α (finite or not) and every subgroup s ≤ α, Nat.card s ∣ Nat.card α. When α is finite this says |s| divides |α|; when α is infinite the right side is 0 and the statement is trivially true.

paper_claims.plain: If G is a finite group and H ≤ G, then |H| divides |G|.

coverage.why: The Lean statement drops the finiteness hypothesis; the extra infinite cases are trivially true since Nat.card α = 0.

flags.explanation: There is no [Finite α] hypothesis. For infinite α, Nat.card α = 0 and divisibility of 0 is trivial. In the finite case the statement is exactly Lagrange, so nothing is lost; the Lean version is only vacuously stronger.
flags.probe_idea: example [Finite α] (s : Subgroup α) : Nat.card s ∣ Nat.card α := stmt s  -- and check Nat.card_eq_fintype_card for agreement with Fintype.card

lint_verdicts.why: Nat.card α = 0 only for infinite α, which the paper excludes. In that case the divisibility is trivially true, so the finite case, the paper's claim, is fully captured.
